commentary.bottom_line: Eight sources endorse training clinicians and staff to explain AI use, disclosures, privacy practices, and opt-out options to patients, but no supplied study tests whether such training improves patient understanding, trust, or consent. The recommendation rests on expert guidance, frameworks, and commentary alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard. Five of the eight endorsements are commentaries, two are CHAI frameworks, and one is a guidance document. The guidance excerpt addresses liability for system failure and misdiagnosis rather than staff training or patient communication, so its support for this recommendation is indirect.

One nursing commentary calls for explaining AI tools to families in clear, non-technical language, and one CHAI playbook calls for plain-language statements in admission paperwork. These endorsements suggest attention to health literacy. No supplied study examines whether trained staff explain AI use accurately to patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy, so the effect in those groups is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: Trials or controlled evaluations should compare trained and untrained staff on patient comprehension of AI use, awareness of opt-out options, consent quality, and trust. These evaluations should also measure staff time and training fidelity in routine workflows.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no data on whether staff training produces accurate explanations for their patients and may need to evaluate it locally.
